title: Nor may we say a physician or letter-reader ‘does not know’ what signs have settled
source_text: LV. Imo non videretur vim vocum invertere, & contra communem hominum sensum loqui, qui diceret quempiam de iis dubitare, atque incertum esse, eaque nescire atque ignorare, quae tamen ex variis signis certo colligit, quaeque vere atque determinate judicat ita esse? An quaecunque signa atque indicia indicent aegrum pleuritide, vel arthritide laborare, de eo tamen semper poterit dici medicus incertus & dubius? An qui syngrapham, sive epistolam ab amico, vel noto accipit, quaecunque signaturae & testimonia concurrant, ut judicet illam ejus esse, eumque revera de hoc certum reddant, nihilominus simpliciter istud nescire dicendus est?
pass_a_gloss: Nay, he would not seem to invert the force of words and speak against the common sense of people who should say that someone doubts concerning those things, and is uncertain, and does not know and is ignorant of them, which nevertheless he certainly gathers from various signs, and which he truly and determinately judges so to be. Or whenever signs and indications indicate that a sick person labors with pleurisy or arthritis, will the physician nevertheless always be able to be called uncertain and doubtful concerning him? Or he who receives a bond or letter from a friend or acquaintance—whatever signatures and testimonies concur so that he judges it to be his, and truly render him certain of this—is he nevertheless to be said simply not to know that?
pass_b_english: Settled medical and documentary judgments are still knowledge in common speech.
Le Blanc’s analogies press Rome’s ‘nescire’ rhetoric as verbal inversion.
